summary: Point-to-multipoint traffic engineering label switched paths may need paths computed before they are signaled. This document extends PCEP so a PCE can compute such paths, with one source and many destinations.

eli5.summary: It lets the route planner compute a tree-shaped route from one starting point to many places at once.

questions: how to compute p2mp lsp paths with pce
how does pce compute p2mp lsp paths
what are p2mp end-points leaf types
subtitle: PCEP extensions that let a path computation element plan a tree-shaped MPLS path from one source to many leaves.

tldr.problem: PCEP, defined in RFC 5440, only asks a path computation element for point-to-point paths. It has no way to request a path for a point-to-multipoint traffic engineering label switched path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds P2MP flags to the RP object, a P2MP END-POINTS object with four leaf types, new objective functions and metrics, new objects such as SERO, SRRO, BNC and UNREACH-DESTINATION, fragmentation, and new error codes.
tldr.outcome: A client can request, reoptimize and change P2MP trees by exchanging PCEP messages. This RFC obsoletes RFC 6006, incorporating its errata, and has since been updated by RFC 9353.

today: RFC 8306 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6006. It has been updated by RFC 9353.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs P2MP Support
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a network path from a network graph and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks it for paths using the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) from RFC 5440. That protocol handles point-to-point (P2P) paths only.

A point-to-multipoint (P2MP) traffic engineering label switched path (TE LSP) delivers from one ingress to several egress routers. It is made of multiple source-to-leaf (S2L) sub-LSPs. The PCE may compute the sub-LSPs separately and combine them, or compute the whole tree in one go.

One request can cover the whole tree or only a subset of the sub-LSPs, and the PCC may split a request across several messages. The PCC decides whether to signal sub-LSPs individually or the entire tree. This document obsoletes RFC 6006 and folds in its errata.
sections.eli5: A normal route planner finds one road from A to B. This one finds a whole tree of roads from A to many places at once.

sections.title: What the Extensions Must Provide
sections.content:
Section 2 lists 15 requirements, numbered as in RFC 5862. Among them: a PCC MUST be able to mark a request as P2MP and ask for objective functions; a request MUST be able to list many destinations; a reply MUST be able to carry a P2MP path; and by default the returned path SHOULD use the compressed format.

A request or reply MUST be able to span a sequence of messages. A single request MUST NOT specify different constraints or quality-of-service needs for different destinations. Existing P2MP LSPs MUST be reoptimizable, leaves MUST be addable and removable, a list of branch nodes MUST be specifiable, and diverse paths MUST be requestable.

A PCE MUST be able to reject a P2MP request and signal non-support, including when it is a back-level implementation.
sections.eli5: Before building anything, the authors wrote a wish list: ask for a tree, name many places, change the tree later, and say no politely when the planner cannot do it.

sections.title: Advertising P2MP Capability
sections.content:
A PCE can announce that it handles P2MP in two ways. In discovery, it sets bit 10 of the OSPF PCE Capability Flags, and IS-IS uses the same flag. PCCs that do not understand the bit ignore it, and PCEs without P2MP support leave it clear.

Otherwise, a PCC can learn this when a PCEP session opens. The RFC defines an optional TLV for the OPEN object, type 6, named "P2MP capable". Its length is 2 bytes and its value defaults to 0. Its presence means the sender can perform P2MP path computation.

A PCE that sets the discovery bit MUST also follow the P2MP END-POINTS procedures to qualify the level of support. When a PCE acting as a PCC starts a session, it SHOULD also indicate its capabilities.
sections.eli5: A planner can put up a sign saying it plans trees, or it can tell you when you first meet.

sections.title: Request and Reply Messages
sections.content:
The RP (Request Parameters) object gets three new flags. The F bit marks a fragmented request or reply that has more pieces coming. The N bit says the message is for P2MP. The E bit says the route is in compressed format. IANA lists them as bits 18, 19 and 20.

The P2MP END-POINTS object has a leaf type field, plus a source address and a list of destinations, in IPv4 (Object-Type 3) or IPv6 (Object-Type 4) form. There are four leaf types: new leaves to add (1), old leaves to remove (2), old leaves that may be reoptimized (3), and old leaves that must stay unchanged (4). A request can mix several END-POINTS objects. For a source with very many destinations, this form can cut the end-points portion of a request by up to 50%.

The PCReq message must carry at least one END-POINTS object, each optionally followed by a list of RRO or SRRO objects. In the PCRep reply, a path is an ERO optionally followed by SERO objects, which use the RSVP-TE explicit route formats to describe each S2L sub-LSP. Object classes 29 (SERO) and 30 (SRRO) are assigned for this.
sections.eli5: A request is a form. It lists where the tree starts and each stop to reach, and tags each stop as new, leaving, may change, or must stay the same.

sections.title: Changing an Existing Tree
sections.content:
To reoptimize, the PCC sets the R bit in the RP object, as for P2P, and MUST put the list of RRO and SRRO objects after each END-POINTS object. These describe the tree as it currently exists.

To add leaves, the PCC builds the request with leaf type 1. To remove leaves, it uses leaf type 2; without one the PCE MUST send Error-Type 17, Error-value 1. When adding or removing, the PCC MUST also give the old leaves using leaf types 3, 4 or both. The RFC works through nine combinations of adding, pruning and full, partial or no reoptimization.

Related requests can be synchronized with an SVEC object, for example when one P2MP LSP is the designated backup of another. Two new SVEC flags exist: P asks for partial path diversity for chosen leaves and D asks for link direction diversity. A Branch Node Capability (BNC) object lists nodes that can, or cannot, act as branch nodes. At most one BNC object may appear per request.
sections.eli5: If you already have a tree, you can say which stops to add, which to drop, which may be re-planned, and which must stay as they are.

sections.title: Objective Functions and Metrics
sections.content:
An objective function tells the PCE what to optimize. RFC 8306 adds two to the six P2P ones from RFC 5541: Shortest-Path Tree (code 7), which minimizes the maximum source-to-leaf cost, and Minimum-Cost Tree (code 8), which minimizes the sum of the costs of all tree links. The default metric is the TE metric when none is given.

Three new METRIC object types hold the sum of metrics over all links of the tree: P2MP IGP metric (T=8), P2MP TE metric (T=9) and P2MP hop count metric (T=10).
sections.eli5: You can ask for the tree where the farthest stop is as close as possible, or the tree with the least total road.

sections.title: Fragmentation, Failures and Errors
sections.content:
Large trees may not fit in one PCEP message. Every piece except the last has the F bit set and all pieces share the same request ID, or response ID for replies. PCEP runs over TCP, so the pieces are assumed to arrive reliably and in order. A receiver may start a timer on the first piece and, if the last never arrives, send Error-Type 18, Error-value 1, "Fragmented request failure".

If a PCE understands the P2MP flag but cannot compute P2MP, it sends a PCErr and the request is cancelled; one that does not understand the flag uses Error-Type 2 (Capability not supported). New values include Error-Type 5, value 7 for policy, and Error-Type 16 values 1 (insufficient memory) and 2 (not capable).

When some destinations cannot be reached, the PCE can say so with the UNREACH-DESTINATION object (class 28) in a PCRep, along with bit 24 in the NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV.
sections.eli5: A huge list gets mailed in several envelopes, all with the same label, with a note on every envelope except the last. If something is wrong, the planner replies with the reason.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
P2MP requests use more CPU and link bandwidth than P2P ones, so unauthorized requests or denial-of-service attacks can disrupt a network. The RFC recommends securing PCEP sessions with TCP-AO or TLS, authenticating requests and replies, and using IP access lists to limit which PCCs may send P2MP requests. PCEP implementations SHOULD support TCP-AO and not use TCP MD5.

On manageability, a PCE may be configured to enable or disable P2MP computation and the advertisement of that capability. Computing a P2MP tree may need more PCE state than P2P, and mass recovery after a major failure could greatly raise the load.
sections.eli5: Planning a tree is hard work, so only trusted callers should be allowed to ask, and the line to the planner should be locked.
